mainTopic: Captive women and claimed כהנים: when one person is believed about herself or about another
overview: The משנה teaches that two captive women are not believed when each says she herself is pure, but they are believed when each testifies for the other. A ברייתא lists four things a captive woman might say about herself and her friend. The גמרא finds that some of its clauses need עדים of captivity while the middle clause needs none. אביי accepts that the ברייתא switches cases this way. רב פפא instead says every clause has עדים of captivity plus a single עד who contradicts her. He shows why each case is needed: we do not suspect she hurt herself to hurt her friend, and she is believed about her friend even when she is clearing herself. A new משנה applies the same idea to two men who claim to be כהנים, and רבי יהודה, רבי אלעזר and רבי שמעון בן הסגן argue about whether one witness is enough. The גמרא then asks why the פרק needs all its similar cases, and begins showing that each one teaches something new. That explanation continues on the next עמוד.

steps.title: Two captive women: believed for each other, not for themselves
steps.stepSummary: The משנה rules that two captive women who each claim to be pure are not believed about themselves. They are believed when each testifies about the other.
steps.simpleTranslation: Two women were taken captive. Each one says, 'I was captured, but I am pure.' They are not believed. But if each testifies that the other is pure, they are believed.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה gives a new rule about two women who were captured. Each one cannot clear herself, but each one can clear the other.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A woman who was captured is suspected of having been violated, which would forbid her to a כהן. Her own word about herself is not enough here. One captive woman is accepted as a witness for another captive woman, so they can clear each other.

keyTerms.meaning: Our משנה
Were taken captive
Pure, meaning not violated by her captors
Believed (plural, feminine)
Testify for each other

steps.whatToRemember: A captive woman's word cannot clear herself, but it can clear another captive woman.

phrases.english: MISHNA:
Two women who were taken captive,
this one says: "I was taken captive, but I am pure,"
phrases.notes: "Pure" here means her captors did not violate her, so she could still marry a כהן.

phrases.english: and that one says: "I was taken captive, but I am pure" —
they are not believed.

phrases.aramaic: וּבִזְמַן שֶׁהֵן מְעִידוֹת זוֹ אֶת זוֹ —
phrases.english: But when they testify for each other —
they are believed.

steps.mimraCoreRuling: Two captive women are not believed when each speaks about herself. They are believed when each testifies about the other.

steps.title: A ברייתא lists four ways a captive woman can speak about herself and her friend
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא lists four statements a captive woman might make about herself and her friend, and says when she is believed in each.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'I am impure and my friend is pure': she is believed. 'I am pure and my friend is impure': she is not believed. 'Both of us are impure': she is believed about herself, not about her friend. 'Both of us are pure': she is believed about her friend, not about herself.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא with four cases about one captive woman talking about herself and her friend.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A clear pattern runs through all four cases. When she makes herself forbidden, she is believed. When she clears her friend, she is believed. When she clears herself or makes her friend forbidden, she is not believed.

keyTerms.meaning: The Talmud's discussion of the משנה
The Rabbis taught; it introduces a ברייתא
Tainted, meaning violated and forbidden to a כהן
My friend, the other captive woman
About herself

steps.whyThisMatters: The rest of the סוגיא tries to work out the exact case this ברייתא is talking about, clause by clause.

phrases.english: GEMARA:
The Rabbis taught:
"I am tainted and my friend is pure" —
she is believed.
"I am pure and my friend is tainted" —
she is not believed.
"I and my friend are tainted" —
she is believed about herself,
but she is not believed about her friend.
"I and my friend are pure" —
she is believed about her friend,
but she is not believed about herself.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Expands on the משנה with more detailed cases.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: She is believed when she forbids herself or clears her friend. She is not believed when she clears herself or forbids her friend.

steps.title: What case is the second clause talking about?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the second clause, 'I am pure and my friend is tainted', and asks what situation it describes.
steps.simpleTranslation: The ברייתא said: 'I am pure and my friend is tainted': she is not believed. What is the case?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes one clause of the ברייתא and asks what situation it describes. This sets up the analysis in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The real question is whether there are עדים that she was captured. That fact changes whether her own word can help her.

keyTerms.meaning: The Master said; it quotes a line from the source just cited
What is the case? What are the circumstances?

phrases.english: The Master said:
"I am pure and my friend is tainted" — she is not believed.
What are the circumstances?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins analyzing the ברייתא.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Are there עדים that she was captured in the case of 'I am pure and my friend is tainted'?

steps.title: The second clause must be a case with עדים
steps.stepSummary: Without עדים she would be believed about herself, since her own words are the only source of the captivity. So the case must have עדים.
steps.simpleTranslation: If there are no witnesses, why is she not believed about herself? She is saying, 'I was captured, and I am pure.' So it must be a case where there are witnesses that she was captured.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers its own question. The second clause must be talking about a case where עדים saw her taken captive.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If no one else knows she was captured, the same mouth that told us about the captivity also tells us she is pure, so she would be believed. The ברייתא says she is not believed about herself. So there must be עדים to the captivity.

keyTerms.meaning: Witnesses, here to the fact that she was captured
Why is she not believed?
It is obvious

steps.confusionAlert: The עדים here saw only that she was captured. They did not see whether she was violated.

phrases.english: If there are no witnesses,
why is she not believed about herself?
She is saying, "I was captured and I am pure"!
phrases.notes: Her own words are the only reason we know she was captured, so the same words can also clear her.

phrases.english: Rather, it is obvious that there are witnesses.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 3.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The second clause must be speaking of a case where there are עדים to the captivity.

steps.title: The middle clause must be a case without עדים
steps.stepSummary: The middle clause only makes sense if there are no עדים. That clashes with the second clause, which needs עדים.
steps.simpleTranslation: Now look at the middle clause: 'I and my friend are tainted': she is believed about herself, not about her friend. If there are witnesses, why is she not believed? It must be that there are no witnesses.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא looks at the next clause and shows it must be a case with no עדים. Now the ברייתא seems to contradict itself, and the גמרא will deal with that next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If עדים saw the friend captured, the friend would already be forbidden, so saying 'she is not believed about her friend' would mean nothing. That phrase must mean the friend stays permitted, which works only without עדים. So one clause needs עדים and another needs no עדים.

keyTerms.meaning: Say the middle clause; look at the next part of the same source
That there is
That there is not

steps.whatToRemember: The second clause of the ברייתא needs עדים, but the middle clause needs no עדים. The גמרא must now explain how the ברייתא can say both.

phrases.english: Say the middle clause:
"I and my friend are tainted" —
she is believed about herself,
but she is not believed about her friend.
And if there are witnesses —
why is she not believed?
phrases.notes: He means about her friend. With witnesses, the friend would already be forbidden anyway.

phrases.english: Rather, it is obvious that there are no witnesses.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Contrasts the middle clause with the conclusion of step 4.
steps.kashyaTarget: The conclusion of step 4 that the ברייתא speaks of a case with עדים
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The middle clause makes sense only without עדים, so the ברייתא seems to switch cases between clauses.

steps.title: The last clause also needs witnesses
steps.stepSummary: In the last clause, where she says 'I and my friend are pure', she is not believed about herself. That only makes sense if there are עדים of captivity.
steps.simpleTranslation: Look at the last clause: 'I and my friend are pure.' She is believed about her friend but not about herself. If there were no witnesses, why wouldn't she be believed about herself? So clearly there are witnesses.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now looks at the last clause of the ברייתא and shows that it must also be talking about a case where עדים saw the captivity. This builds pressure for the challenge that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If no one saw her taken captive, her own words are the only source of the problem, so she would be believed when she says she is pure. Since the ברייתא says she is not believed about herself, there must be עדים of captivity. Now the last clause has עדים while the middle clause does not, and that clash sets up the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: The last clause of a ברייתא or משנה
She is believed
It is obvious
Why?

phrases.english: Say the last clause:
"I and my friend are pure"
she is believed about her friend,
but she is not believed about herself.
And if there are no witnesses,
phrases.notes: He means witnesses who saw that she was taken captive.

phrases.english: why is she not believed about herself?
Rather, it is obvious that there are witnesses.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Extends the analysis to the last clause and shows it also requires עדים.
steps.kashyaTarget: The idea that the ברייתא describes one consistent case
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Not believing her about herself only makes sense if there are עדים of captivity, so the last clause has עדים while the middle clause does not.

steps.title: An odd pattern: witnesses, no witnesses, witnesses
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא is surprised: the first and last clauses have עדים, but the middle one does not?
steps.simpleTranslation: So the first and last clauses are talking about a case with witnesses, and the middle clause is talking about a case without witnesses?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא states the problem out loud. It would be strange for one ברייתא to switch cases in the middle and then switch back.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally the clauses of a ברייתא share the same background facts. Here the first and last clauses need עדים, but the middle clause needs no עדים. The גמרא asks whether a ברייתא can really be built this way.

keyTerms.meaning: The first clause
The middle clause
Where there are
Where there are not

phrases.english: The first and last clauses are where there are witnesses,
and the middle clause is where there are no witnesses?!

steps.triggerLanguage: רֵישָׁא וְסֵיפָא דְּאִיכָּא עֵדִים, מְצִיעֲתָא דְּלֵיכָּא עֵדִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: States the clash that step 6 produced.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A ברייתא should not switch its background facts back and forth between clauses.

steps.title: אביי: Yes, the ברייתא really switches
steps.stepSummary: אביי accepts the odd pattern. The first and last clauses have עדים, and the middle clause has none.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: Yes. The first and last clauses are where there are witnesses, and the middle clause is where there are no witnesses.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי answers by simply agreeing that the ברייתא does switch cases. He does not try to explain the problem away.
steps.deeperAnalysis: אביי holds that it is fine for a ברייתא to set different clauses in different situations. Each clause is read in the case where its ruling makes sense.

keyTerms.meaning: Yes
אביי, an אמורא

phrases.english: אביי said: Yes.
The first and last clauses are where there are witnesses,
the middle clause is where there are no witnesses.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 7 by accepting it.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Accepts the premise: the clauses really describe different cases
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A ברייתא must keep one background case throughout.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא can mix cases: the first and last clauses have עדים, and the middle has none.

steps.title: רב פפא: Witnesses throughout, plus one opposing witness
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא says the whole ברייתא has עדים of captivity, plus a single עד who says the opposite of what the woman says. In the first case she forbids herself, and her friend is permitted by her word.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said: The whole ברייתא is where there are witnesses of captivity, and there is also one witness who says the reverse. She said, 'I am tainted and my friend is pure,' and one witness told her, 'You are pure and your friend is tainted.' She made herself forbidden by her own words, and her friend is permitted by her word.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא offers a different answer that keeps the ברייתא consistent. Every clause has עדים of captivity, and what changes is that a single עד contradicts the woman.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When she calls herself tainted, her own admission forbids her, even though the עד says she is pure. Her friend is still permitted because of what she said, even though the עד says the friend is tainted.

keyTerms.meaning: A single witness
Reverses, says the opposite
She made herself a 'forbidden piece', forbidding herself by her own admission
On the basis of her word

steps.confusionAlert: There are two kinds of witnesses here. The עדים saw the captivity. The עד אחד is a different, single witness who argues with the woman about who is pure.

phrases.aramaic: רַב פָּפָּא אָמַר: כּוּלָּהּ דְּאִיכָּא עֵדִים,
phrases.english: רב פפא said: The whole of it is where there are witnesses,
and there is one witness who says the reverse.
She said: "I am tainted and my friend is pure,"
and one witness said to her:
"You are pure and your friend is tainted."
She made herself
a forbidden piece,
phrases.notes: A picture phrase: by admitting she is tainted, she forbids herself, whatever the witness says.

phrases.english: and her friend is permitted by her word.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב פָּפָּא אָמַר: כּוּלָּהּ דְּאִיכָּא עֵדִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a second answer to step 7, instead of אביי's.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefines the case so that all the clauses share the same background
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The middle clause must be a case without עדים.
steps.terutzMaskana: All the clauses have עדים of captivity, and a single opposing עד explains the different rulings.

steps.title: רב פפא's reading of 'I am pure, my friend is tainted'
steps.stepSummary: When she calls herself pure and the single עד says the reverse, she cannot permit herself because there are עדים of captivity. Her friend is permitted by the עד's word.
steps.simpleTranslation: If she says, 'I am pure and my friend is tainted,' and one witness tells her, 'You are tainted and your friend is pure': as for her, since there are witnesses of captivity, it is not in her power to permit herself. Her friend is permitted by the witness's word.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא continues his reading and applies it to the second case of the ברייתא, 'I am pure and my friend is tainted.' He shows that this case also has עדים of captivity.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Because עדים saw her taken captive, her own claim that she is pure cannot help her. Her friend is permitted, but this time by the single עד, not by her. רב פפא will go on to explain the other two cases the same way.

keyTerms.meaning: It is not in her power
Since
On the basis of the witness's word

steps.whatToRemember: אביי: the clauses switch between cases with עדים and without. רב פפא: every clause has עדים of captivity, and a single opposing עד explains the rulings. A woman's admission can forbid herself, but it cannot permit herself once there are עדים of captivity.

phrases.english: "I am pure and my friend is tainted,"
and one witness said to her:
"You are tainted and your friend is pure."
As for her, since there are witnesses,
phrases.notes: These are the witnesses who saw the captivity, not the single witness.

phrases.english: it is not in her power to permit herself;
her friend is permitted by the witness's word.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיהִי, כֵּיוָן דְּאִיכָּא עֵדִים — לָאו כָּל כְּמִינַהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues רב פפא's reading by applying it to the second case, 'I am pure and my friend is tainted'.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Applies the redefined case to the remaining clause
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Under אביי's reading, the clauses switch between cases with עדים and without עדים.
steps.terutzMaskana: With עדים of captivity she cannot permit herself, and her friend is permitted through the single עד.

steps.title: Third case: she says both are impure, the עד says both are pure
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא applies his reading to the third case. She says 'I and my friend are impure.' One עד says 'both of you are pure.' She forbids herself, and her friend is permitted by the עד's word.
steps.simpleTranslation: If she says 'I and my friend are impure,' and one witness tells her 'You and your friend are pure,' she has made herself forbidden. Her friend is permitted because of the witness.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא keeps going through the ברייתא with his reading. Now he explains the case where the woman calls both of them impure.
steps.deeperAnalysis: About herself, her own words count: once she says she is impure (forbidden to a כהן), she has made herself forbidden. About her friend, she is contradicted by a single עד who says the friend is pure. The friend is permitted based on that עד.

keyTerms.meaning: 'A piece of prohibition': someone who has made herself forbidden by her own words
A single witness
'By the mouth of', meaning based on someone's word
Here: forbidden / permitted to marry a כֹּהֵן after captivity

phrases.english: "I and my friend are impure,"
and one witness said to her:
"You and your friend are pure":
she has made herself a "piece of prohibition,"
phrases.notes: By saying she is impure, she has locked herself into being forbidden, whatever the witness says.

phrases.english: her friend is permitted by the word of the witness.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲנִי וַחֲבֶרְתִּי טְמֵאָה וְאָמַר לַהּ עֵד אֶחָד אַתְּ וַחֲבֶרְתֵּךְ טְהוֹרָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues רב פפא's case-by-case reading of the ברייתא from Steps 9-10.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Re-reading the case: every clause has עדים of captivity plus one contradicting עד
steps.terutzMaskana: She forbids herself by her own word, and her friend is permitted by the עד.

steps.title: Why do we need this case? It repeats the first clause
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the ברייתא needs this case, since the same rules were already taught in the first clause.
steps.simpleTranslation: Why do I need this too? It is the same as the first clause!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the ברייתא for repeating itself. The same rules seem to come out of the earlier cases.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier cases already taught two things: a woman who calls herself impure is forbidden by her own word, and her friend can be permitted by one person's word even when someone contradicts it. So this third case seems to teach nothing new.

keyTerms.meaning: 'Why do I need this too?': the ברייתא seems to repeat itself
'This is the same as the first clause'

phrases.english: Why do I need this too?
This is the same as the first clause!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the case just explained in Step 11 as a repeat.
steps.kashyaTarget: The third case of the ברייתא (both impure / both pure)
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא does not repeat itself for no reason. Since its rules were already taught, this case looks pointless.

steps.title: We might have thought she was sacrificing herself to hurt her friend
steps.stepSummary: The case is needed. Otherwise we might think both women are really pure, and she only called herself impure 'like שמשון' so that her words against her friend would be believed. The ברייתא teaches that we do not think this way.
steps.simpleTranslation: You might have said: both of them are really pure, and she only said this to 'die with the Philistines.' So the ברייתא teaches us otherwise.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question from Step 12. It shows that this case blocks a mistake we could have made.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Someone might suspect that she hurt herself on purpose so that people would believe her claim against her friend. That is what שמשון did when he died together with his enemies. If so, we would ignore her words about herself too and call both of them pure. The ברייתא teaches that we do not suspect this, so she stays forbidden.

keyTerms.meaning: 'You might have said': introduces a mistaken idea the source comes to block
'Let me die with the Philistines': hurting yourself in order to hurt someone else
'It teaches us': the new point this source makes

steps.confusionAlert: Don't think the ברייתא is now saying both are pure. The 'Philistines' idea is the mistake being rejected. She stays forbidden, and only her friend is permitted.

phrases.english: You might have said:
these two are both pure,
and the reason she said this
is "Let me die with the Philistines"
that she was doing.
So it teaches us otherwise.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the 'why do I need it' question of Step 12.
steps.terutzResolutionType: מהו דתימא: the case blocks a mistaken idea
steps.terutzHavaAmina: She called herself impure only to make her claim against her friend believable, so both are pure.
steps.terutzMaskana: We do not suspect a 'die with the Philistines' plan. She is forbidden by her own words.

steps.title: Fourth case: she says both are pure, the עד says both are impure
steps.stepSummary: She says 'I and my friend are pure.' One עד says 'both of you are impure.' Since there are עדים of captivity, she cannot permit herself, but her friend is permitted by her word.
steps.simpleTranslation: If she says 'I and my friend are pure,' and one witness tells her 'You and your friend are impure': she cannot permit herself, since there are witnesses that she was captured. Her friend is permitted by her word.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא explains the last case of the ברייתא with his reading.
steps.deeperAnalysis: About herself, she cannot clear her own name, because עדים saw that she was taken captive. About her friend, her word counts and permits the friend, even though one עד says the opposite.

keyTerms.meaning: 'It is not in her power': her word cannot do this
Here: the witnesses who saw that she was taken captive

phrases.english: "I and my friend are pure,"
and one witness said to her:
"You and your friend are impure":
as for her, since there are witnesses,
phrases.notes: These are the witnesses that she was taken captive, not the single witness.

phrases.english: it is not in her power to permit herself.
Her friend is permitted by her word.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲנִי וַחֲבֶרְתִּי טְהוֹרָה וְאָמַר לָהּ עֵד אֶחָד אַתְּ וַחֲבֶרְתֵּךְ טְמֵאָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues רב פפא's reading with the fourth and last case.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Re-reading the case: every clause has עדים of captivity plus one contradicting עד
steps.terutzMaskana: She cannot permit herself, but her friend is permitted by her word.

steps.title: Why do we need this case? It repeats the very first case
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא again asks why this case is needed, since its rules were already taught at the very start of the ברייתא.
steps.simpleTranslation: Why do I need this too? It is the same as the first part of the first clause!
steps.whatsHappening: The same 'why repeat it?' challenge is now aimed at the last case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier cases already taught that she cannot permit herself when there are עדים of captivity, and that her word can permit her friend even against one עד. So this case seems to add nothing.

keyTerms.meaning: 'The beginning of the beginning': the very first part of the ברייתא

phrases.english: Why do I need this too?
This is the same as the very first part of the first clause!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Same kind of challenge as Step 12, now on the fourth case.
steps.kashyaTarget: The fourth case of the ברייתא (both pure / both impure)
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Both of its rules were already taught earlier, so the case looks extra.

steps.title: She is believed about her friend even when she is helping herself
steps.stepSummary: The case is needed. We might have thought she is believed about her friend only when she also hurts herself, but not when she is trying to make herself fit. The ברייתא teaches that she is believed about her friend either way.
steps.simpleTranslation: You might have said: she is believed only when she disqualifies herself, but when she is making herself fit, say she is not believed. So the ברייתא teaches us otherwise.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question from Step 15. It shows that this case blocks another possible mistake.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When she calls herself impure, her honesty looks clear, so trusting her about her friend makes sense. When she calls herself pure, she is helping herself, and we might distrust everything she says. The ברייתא teaches that her words about her friend are judged on their own, so the friend is still permitted.

keyTerms.meaning: She is believed
She makes herself unfit (forbidden to a כֹּהֵן)
She makes herself fit (permitted to a כֹּהֵן)

steps.whatToRemember: In רב פפא's reading, each woman's statement is judged in two separate parts. About herself: if she calls herself impure, she is forbidden. If she calls herself pure, she cannot permit herself against the עדים of captivity. About her friend: one person's word permits the friend. The last two cases teach that we don't suspect a 'Philistines' trick, and that she is believed about her friend even when she is helping herself.

phrases.english: You might have said:
when is she believed?
Only where she disqualifies herself;
but where she makes herself fit,
say she is not believed.
So it teaches us otherwise.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the 'why do I need it' question of Step 15.
steps.terutzResolutionType: מהו דתימא: the case blocks a mistaken idea
steps.terutzHavaAmina: She is believed about her friend only when she also hurts herself, not when she is helping herself.
steps.terutzMaskana: Her word about her friend counts even when she is trying to make herself fit.

steps.title: Two men who each claim to be a כהן
steps.stepSummary: Two unknown men each saying 'I am a כהן' are not believed about themselves, but they are believed when each testifies about the other.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: In the same way, two men: this one says 'I am a כהן' and that one says 'I am a כהן.' They are not believed. But when they testify about each other, they are believed.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה opens. It gives the case of two strangers who claim to be כהנים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A person's own word about himself is not enough to give him the status of a כהן. But each man can serve as a witness for the other, and then both are accepted. The opening word וכן ('and likewise') ties this to the earlier cases in the פרק, where one person is believed about someone else.

keyTerms.meaning: Short for מַתְנִיתִין, 'our משנה.' A new משנה starts here.
A descendant of אהרן, who has special privileges and restrictions.
Believed; their word is accepted.
They testify about each other.

phrases.english: MISHNAH:
And likewise, two men,
this one says, 'I am a כהן,'
and that one says, 'I am a כהן' —
they are not believed.

phrases.aramaic: וּבִזְמַן שֶׁהֵן מְעִידִין זֶה אֶת זֶה —
phrases.english: But when they testify about each other —
they are believed.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכֵן שְׁנֵי אֲנָשִׁים, זֶה אוֹמֵר ״כֹּהֵן אֲנִי״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new משנה. It parallels the earlier case of two women, where each is believed about the other but not about herself.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A man is not believed when he says he himself is a כהן, but two men are believed when each testifies that the other is a כהן.

steps.title: רבי יהודה requires more than one witness
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהודה rules that we do not give someone the status of a כהן based on only one witness.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהודה says: We do not raise someone to כהונה based on one witness.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהודה disagrees with the first opinion in the משנה. He holds that one witness is not enough.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the first opinion, each man is a single witness for the other, and that works. רבי יהודה says becoming a כהן needs two witnesses, so this mutual testimony is not enough.

keyTerms.meaning: We 'raise up' someone to כהונה, meaning we treat him as a כהן.
A single witness.

phrases.english: רבי יהודה says:
We do not raise someone to כהונה
based on one witness.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי יְהוּדָה אוֹמֵר: אֵין מַעֲלִין לִכְהוּנָּה עַל פִּי עֵד אֶחָד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Disagrees with the first opinion, which accepts each man's single testimony for the other.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Two witnesses are needed to treat someone as a כהן.

steps.title: רבי אלעזר limits the rule to when there are challengers
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלעזר says one witness is not enough only when people are challenging the claim. When nobody challenges it, one witness is enough.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אלעזר said: When is this so? Where there are challengers. But where there are no challengers, we raise someone to כהונה based on one witness.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אלעזר narrows the rule that one witness is not enough. He says it applies only in a certain situation.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If people are protesting that this man is not a כהן, we need two witnesses. If nobody protests, a single witness is enough. So the need for two witnesses depends on whether the claim is being challenged.

keyTerms.meaning: When? It introduces a limit on a rule.
Challengers; people who protest or question someone's status.

phrases.english: רבי אלעזר said: When is this so?
Where there are challengers.
But where there are no challengers —

phrases.aramaic: מַעֲלִין לִכְהוּנָּה עַל פִּי עֵד אֶחָד.
phrases.english: we raise someone to כהונה based on one witness.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר: אֵימָתַי — בִּמְקוֹם שֶׁיֵּשׁ עוֹרְרִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Limits רבי יהודה's rule to cases where the claim is challenged.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Two witnesses are needed only when there are challengers. Without challengers, one witness is enough.

steps.title: One witness is enough to establish a כהן
steps.stepSummary: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל, quoting רבי שמעון בן הסגן, rules that one witness is enough to treat someone as a כהן.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says in the name of רבי שמעון בן הסגן: We raise someone to כהונה based on one witness.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה ends with one more opinion. It fully allows a single witness.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Unlike רבי יהודה, this opinion gives no condition. One witness is enough to treat someone as a כהן.

keyTerms.meaning: In the name of; quoting someone.
The deputy כהן גדול.

steps.whatToRemember: The משנה gives a range of views: one witness is fine (first opinion and רבי שמעון בן הסגן), two are needed (רבי יהודה), or two are needed only if there are challengers (רבי אלעזר).

phrases.english: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says
in the name of רבי שמעון בן הסגן:

phrases.aramaic: מַעֲלִין לִכְהוּנָּה עַל פִּי עֵד אֶחָד.
phrases.english: We raise someone to כהונה based on one witness.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבָּן שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן גַּמְלִיאֵל אוֹמֵר מִשּׁוּם רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן הַסְּגָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a final view that disagrees with רבי יהודה and allows one witness with no condition.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A single witness is enough to establish someone as a כהן.

steps.title: Why does the פרק need all these cases?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the פרק lists so many cases that all seem to teach the same idea.
steps.simpleTranslation: גמרא: Why do I need all of these?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins with a challenge. The פרק has many cases that all seem to follow one rule, הפה שאסר הוא הפה שהתיר, so why list them all?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פרק repeats the same basic idea several times: the field, the witnesses, the woman, the captives, and now the כהנים. The גמרא assumes the משנה does not repeat itself for no reason, so each case must teach something new.

keyTerms.meaning: Short for גְּמָרָא; the discussion of the משנה begins.
Why do I need it? This asks why something is written when it seems repeated.
The mouth that forbade is the mouth that permitted. The person whose word created the problem can also remove it.

phrases.english: GEMARA:
Why do I need all of these?
phrases.notes: 'All of these' means all the similar cases taught across this פרק, not only the case of the כהנים.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens the גמרא's discussion by questioning why the פרק repeats so many cases.
steps.kashyaTarget: The many cases of the פרק that seem to teach one principle.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If they all teach הפה שאסר הוא הפה שהתיר, one case should have been enough.

steps.title: The field case alone would not teach the witnesses case
steps.stepSummary: Each case is needed. From the field case alone, we might think he is believed because of the money angle. Witnesses, who have no money angle, might not be believed.
steps.simpleTranslation: They are needed. If the משנה had taught only the case where רבי יהושע agrees, we would say he is believed because there is a money matter involved. But witnesses, where no money matter is involved, we might say are not believed.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that all the cases are needed. It starts showing why the field case alone would not be enough.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the field case, the man admits the field once belonged to the other person's father. That admission has a money side to it, so we might think that is why he is believed. Witnesses who confirm their signatures have no money involved, so without their own case we might not believe them.

keyTerms.meaning: They are needed; each case teaches something the others do not.
רבי יהושע agrees. This points to the earlier משנה about a field.
A money matter; a financial side to the claim.
I might say no; I might have thought the rule does not apply.

phrases.english: They are needed,
for if it had taught only 'רבי יהושע agrees,'
phrases.notes: This is the earlier משנה: 'This field was your father's, and I bought it from him.' רבי יהושע agrees he is believed.

phrases.english: I would say that is because there is a money matter involved.
But witnesses, where there is no money matter involved —
phrases.notes: This is the earlier משנה about witnesses who say 'this is our handwriting, but we were forced to sign.'

phrases.english: I might say they are not believed.

steps.triggerLanguage: צְרִיכִי, דְּאִי תְּנָא מוֹדֶה רַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins answering the question of why all the cases are needed.
steps.terutzResolutionType: צריכותא: showing that each case teaches something the others cannot.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: From the field case alone, one might think the reason he is believed is the money matter, so witnesses with no money matter would not be believed.
steps.terutzMaskana: The witnesses case is needed to teach that they are believed even without any money matter.

steps.title: The witnesses case alone would not teach the field case
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא starts the reverse argument. From the witnesses case alone, we might think they are believed because they speak about others, while a man speaking about himself might not be.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if it had taught only the witnesses, I would say they are believed because their words concern others. But he, whose words concern himself,
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now shows why the witnesses case alone would not be enough. This sentence is not finished here; it continues on the next עמוד.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Witnesses testify about other people's matters, so they have no personal interest, and that may be why they are believed. The man in the field case is talking about his own field, so we might suspect him. The conclusion of this thought comes next.

keyTerms.meaning: Concerning others; about the rest of the world.
Concerning himself.
He. This refers to the man in the field case.

steps.confusionAlert: The sentence breaks off in the middle. The words 'I might say he is not believed' come right after this, at the start of the next עמוד.

phrases.english: And if it had taught only the witnesses,
I would say they are believed because their words concern others,
but he, whose words concern himself,
phrases.notes: 'He' is the man who says he bought the field. The sentence finishes on the next עמוד.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the reverse side of the explanation of why both cases are needed.
steps.terutzResolutionType: צריכותא: showing that each case teaches something the others cannot.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: From the witnesses case alone, one might think they are believed only because they speak about others, while a person speaking about himself would not be believed.
steps.terutzMaskana: The field case is needed to teach that even someone speaking about his own matter is believed. This conclusion is finished on the next עמוד.
